assignments.name: Build a complete HTML document
assignments.description:
## Give your page its proper skeleton **What you are making:** a complete HTML document — the same skeleton every professional web page in the world starts from, with a name that appears on the browser tab. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-doc-structure-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-doc-structure-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-doc-structure-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your file In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There is no code file yet — you create it yourself.** For this assignment, create this file: - `index.html` **To make a file in VS Code:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly — for example `index.html` — and press **Enter**. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** replace what is in `index.html` with a complete, properly shaped document. 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Click anywhere in that big area. 3. Press **Ctrl + A** *(Mac: Command + A)*. Everything in the file turns blue — it is now selected. 4. Press **Backspace** *(the key above Enter, sometimes marked ←)*. The file is now empty. This is meant to happen. 5. Type the whole thing below, exactly as it is written. The spaces at the start of the indented lines are there to make it readable — copy them if you can, but nothing breaks if they are off by one. ```html My Page

Hello

This page has a proper skeleton now.

``` **What each piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `` | Tells the browser *this is a modern web page*. Always the first line. Note the exclamation mark, and no space after `` … `` | Wraps the entire page. Everything else lives inside these two. | | `lang="en"` | Says the page is written in English. | | `` … `` | Information **about** the page. Visitors never see what is in here. | | `` | Tells the browser which alphabet to use. It is a lonely tag — no closing partner. | | `My Page` | The name shown on the **browser tab** at the top of the window. | | `` … `` | Everything people actually **see**. From now on, your work goes in here. | Tags shut from the inside out. `` closes before `` opens, and `` comes last of all — like boxes packed inside boxes. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change `My Page` to any name, and change the heading and paragraph words. Every tag, and the line ``, must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Look at the **tab along the top of the browser window**. It should read **My Page** — not `index.html`. That is your `` doing its work. In the page itself you see the heading and the paragraph from inside `<body>`. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Tab still says `index.html`? The `<title>` line is missing, is outside `<head>`, or the file was not saved. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add the full HTML skeleton" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The browser tab still says `index.html` | The `<title>` is missing or sits outside `<head>` | `<title>My Page` must be between `` and `` | | Your heading appears in the browser tab instead of on the page | It was typed inside `` | `<title>` holds the tab name only — your `<h1>` belongs between `<body>` and `</body>` | | Red cross on "has doctype" | The first line is mistyped | It reads `<!doctype html>` — exclamation mark straight after `<`, no space | | VS Code draws a wiggly red line under `</html>` | A closing tag is missing or out of order | Check the order at the bottom: `</body>` then `</html>` | | The word `charset` shows up on the page | The `<meta>` line lost one of its angle brackets | The whole line must sit between `<` and `>` | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] The very first line is `<!doctype html>` - [ ] There is an `<html lang="en">` and a matching `</html>` at the end - [ ] There is a `<head>` … `</head>` pair - [ ] `<title>` … `` sits inside the `` - [ ] There is a `` … `` pair with your heading inside it - [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab) - [ ] The browser tab shows your title, not `index.html`

assignments.name: Build a form
assignments.description:
## Build a sign-up form people can type in

**What you are making:** a small sign-up form with a name box, an email box, a tick box and a button — the same set of parts behind every sign-up page you have ever filled in.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-form-page-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-form-page-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-form-page-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project and create your file

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** This project starts empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There is no code file yet — you make it yourself**, then paste in the starter below.

For this assignment, create this file:

- `index.html`

**To make a file in VS Code:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly — `index.html` — and press **Enter**.

Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, **paste in exactly this**, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Your work for this lesson goes here, between <body> and </body>. -->
  </body>
</html>
```

This is the **starter skeleton** every web page needs: the `<head>` holds information about the page, and the `<body>` holds everything people actually see. You do your work **between `<body>` and `</body>`** in the next step.

*Tip: in an empty `.html` file you can also type a single `!` and press **Tab**, and VS Code writes this skeleton for you — the shortcut is called Emmet. Pasting the block above is the sure route, since it already includes this lesson's exact starting point.*

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** put a working sign-up form on the page.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**.
3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line.
4. Type this:

```html
<form>
  <label>Name <input type="text"></label>
  <label>Email <input type="email"></label>
  <label>Subscribe to updates <input type="checkbox"></label>
  <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
</form>
```

**What each piece means:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<form>` … `</form>` | Wraps the whole thing and marks it as one form. |
| `<input>` | A box the visitor types in. A lonely tag — there is **no** `</input>`. |
| `type="text"` | An ordinary typing box. |
| `type="email"` | A box that expects an email address. |
| `type="checkbox"` | A small square you can tick. |
| `<label>` … `</label>` | The words next to a box. Wrapping the box **inside** the label joins the two together, so clicking the words puts the cursor in the box. |
| `<button type="submit">` | The button that sends the form. The words between the tags are what is printed on it. |

Every box needs a label. A box with no label is a guessing game for the visitor, and unusable for anybody using a screen reader.

Clicking **Sign up** will appear to do nothing, or will blink the page. That is correct — there is nowhere yet to send the answers to.

**Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> You may change the words *Name*, *Email*, *Subscribe to updates* and *Sign up*. Keep the `<form>`, the three `<input>` boxes, the `<label>` round each one, and the `<button>`.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see the words *Name* with a typing box beside it, *Email* with another box, *Subscribe to updates* with a small empty square, and a button reading **Sign up**. Click inside the first box and type your name — the letters appear. Now click the **words** *Subscribe to updates*: the square should tick itself. That is the label doing its job.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

Boxes missing? Check each `<input>` sits between `<form>` and `</form>`, and that the file was saved.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add a sign-up form"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

assignments.description:
## Play a video inside your own page

**What you are making:** a page with a YouTube video playing inside it — a window cut into your page that shows another website through it.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-media-page-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-media-page-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-media-page-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project and create your file

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** This project starts empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There is no code file yet — you make it yourself**, then paste in the starter below.

For this assignment, create this file:

- `index.html`

**To make a file in VS Code:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly — `index.html` — and press **Enter**.

Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, **paste in exactly this**, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*:

```html
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="utf-8" />
    <title>My Page</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <!-- Your work for this lesson goes here, between <body> and </body>. -->
  </body>
</html>
```

This is the **starter skeleton** every web page needs: the `<head>` holds information about the page, and the `<body>` holds everything people actually see. You do your work **between `<body>` and `</body>`** in the next step.

*Tip: in an empty `.html` file you can also type a single `!` and press **Tab**, and VS Code writes this skeleton for you — the shortcut is called Emmet. Pasting the block above is the sure route, since it already includes this lesson's exact starting point.*

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** put a playable video on your page.

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**.
3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line.
4. Type this as **one single line**. It is long — let it run off the edge of the screen and do not press **Enter** in the middle of it:

```html
<iframe width="560" height="315" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/aqz-KE-bpKQ" title="A video" allowfullscreen></iframe>
```

**What each piece means:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `<iframe>` … `</iframe>` | A window that shows **another web page inside yours**. Nothing goes between the two tags, but the closing tag is still required. |
| `width="560"` and `height="315"` | The size of that window, measured in screen dots called pixels. |
| `src="…"` | The address of the page to show inside the window. |
| `/embed/aqz-KE-bpKQ` | The part after `/embed/` is the video's own code. |
| `title="A video"` | A short description, read aloud to people using a screen reader. |
| `allowfullscreen` | Lets a viewer blow the video up to fill the screen. It stands alone — no `=` and no quotes after it. |

**To use a video of your own instead:**

1. Open YouTube in your browser and start any video.
2. Look at the address at the very top of the browser. It reads something like `https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aqz-KE-bpKQ`.
3. The code is the part straight after `v=` — here, `aqz-KE-bpKQ`. If there is an `&` after it, stop at the `&`.
4. Replace `aqz-KE-bpKQ` in your `src` with that code, keeping `https://www.youtube.com/embed/` in front of it.

The address must say `/embed/`, not `/watch?v=`. A `/watch?v=` address gives you an empty grey rectangle.

**Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> You may use any video code you like, and any numbers for `width` and `height`. The tag must stay an `<iframe>` with a `src` that starts `https://www.youtube.com/embed/`.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see a black rectangle with a large play button in the middle. Click it — the video plays, inside your own page.

Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.

An empty grey or white rectangle? The address uses `/watch?v=` instead of `/embed/`, or your computer is not connected to the internet — this one needs a connection.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Embed a YouTube video"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| An empty grey or white rectangle | The address uses `/watch?v=` instead of `/embed/` | The `src` must read `https://www.youtube.com/embed/CODE` |
| The words *Video unavailable* inside the rectangle | That video's owner does not allow embedding | Pick a different video and swap its code into the `src` |
| Nothing at all appears on the page | `</iframe>` is missing | The closing tag is required even though nothing sits between the tags |
| The video is tiny, or far too big | `width` and `height` are measured in pixels | Change 560 and 315 to other numbers and reload |
| Red cross on "has an <iframe>" | The line was broken in two by pressing **Enter** | It must be one unbroken line starting `<iframe ` |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] There is an `<iframe` … `</iframe>` on the page
- [ ] Its `src` starts with `https://www.youtube.com/embed/`
- [ ] There is a video code straight after `/embed/`
- [ ] The iframe sits between `<body>` and `</body>`
- [ ] The file is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] The video actually plays when you click it in the browser

Look back at the `.card` rule you have written. Click at the **end** of the line `padding: 24px;` and press **Enter** for a new line. 6. Type these three lines. They must stay **inside** the same pair of curly brackets as the rest of the `.card` rule: ```css display: flex; flex-direction: column; align-items: center; ``` **Stage 6 — the photograph and the words** 7. Click at the very bottom of the file, press **Enter** twice, and type this: ```css .avatar { width: 120px; height: 120px; border-radius: 50%; } .card p { text-align: center; color: #666666; } ``` 8. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each new piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `#eef1f5` | A colour written as a code rather than a word. The `#` is followed by six characters saying how much red, how much green and how much blue. `#ffffff` is white, `#000000` is black. Codes let you pick shades no word exists for. | | `font-family: Arial, sans-serif;` | Which lettering to use. If Arial is missing from the computer, the browser falls back to any plain `sans-serif` lettering. | | `padding: 24px;` | Space **inside** the box, between its border and its contents. This is what makes a card feel roomy rather than cramped. | | `border: 1px solid #cccccc;` | Three things in one line: how thick the outline is, what style it is, and what colour. | | `border-radius: 12px;` | Rounds off the corners. On the photograph, `50%` rounds it the whole way into a circle. | | `margin: 40px auto;` | Space **outside** the box: 40 dots above and below, and `auto` on the left and right. That `auto` is what centres the card on the page. | | `display: flex;` with `flex-direction: column;` | Puts the card's three contents in a single column, one under the other. | | `align-items: center;` | Lines them up down the middle of the card. | | `.card p` | Two names with a space between them means "a paragraph **inside** a card" — not every paragraph on the page. | | `max-width: 100%;` | Stops the 300-dot card hanging over the edge when the window is narrower than 300 dots. | **One spelling warning.** CSS writes it `center`, the American way. `centre` is not a word any browser knows, and a line containing it is thrown away in silence. This applies to `align-items: center;` and `text-align: center;` both. > Change whatever you like: the colours, the name, the words, the numbers, the picture. Four things must survive, because the checker looks for them: the `` line in `index.html`, a `color` somewhere in `style.css`, a `padding` somewhere in `style.css`, and `display: flex;` inside the `.card` rule. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see a pale grey-blue page. Near the top of it, in the middle, sits a white box with rounded corners and a thin grey outline. Inside the box, from top to bottom: a **round** photograph, a name in bold underneath it, and a grey line of text under that. Everything is centred, with a comfortable band of space inside the box's edges. 5. Check the card behaves when the window is small. If the browser window fills your screen, click the **middle button of the three at the top-right corner** (between the **—** and the **✕**). *(Mac: press **Control + Command + F**.)* 6. Move the mouse pointer onto the **right-hand edge** of the window until it becomes a double-headed arrow. **Press and hold** the left mouse button and move the mouse to the **left**. 7. The card stays 300 dots wide and stays in the middle while there is room for it. Once the window is narrower than the card itself, the card shrinks with the window instead of hanging off the side — that is `max-width: 100%`. Let go of the button and drag the edge back out. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. No colour at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Build and style a profile card" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The page is plain white and nothing is styled | `index.html` is not connected to `style.css` | Inside `` there must be `` | | The card sits against the left-hand edge of the page | The `auto` in the margin is missing | It must read `margin: 40px auto;` — `auto` is what centres it | | The photograph is a square, not a circle | `border-radius: 50%;` is not inside the `.avatar` rule | It must sit between the `{` and `}` of `.avatar`, and the picture must be as tall as it is wide | | The contents huddle against the left of the card | `center` was spelled the British way | A browser only understands `center`. `centre` is ignored | | Red cross on "lays out with flex or grid" | `display: flex;` landed outside the `.card` brackets | It must be between the `{` and `}` of `.card`. Save, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has `` inside `` - [ ] `style.css` sets a `color` on `body` - [ ] `style.css` has `padding: 24px;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `style.css` has `display: flex;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `center` is spelled the American way everywhere in `style.css` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] The card shows in your browser as a white rounded box with a round photograph

assignments.name: Your first push
assignments.description:
## Learn the routine you will use every time

**What you are making:** a file called `hello.txt` with your name in it, handed in for checking. The file is tiny on purpose. The point of this assignment is not the file — it is learning the nine steps you will repeat for **every** assignment in this course.

**Time:** about 40 minutes the first time. It gets faster every time after this.

---

### Before you start

You need three things already done. If any is missing, go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and finish it first:

- **VS Code** is installed — the app with the blue icon.
- **Git Bash** is installed (Windows), or you have found the **Terminal** app (Mac).
- You have a **GitHub account**, and you have run `gh auth login` so your computer can talk to it.

You also need the folder you made in the **Meet the terminal** lesson: **Documents → `lacefi-academy`**.

---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

You are now inside your course folder. Every assignment in this course lives here.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are, so you do not have to tell it.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

GitHub has made you your own private copy of this assignment. Now you bring it down onto your computer. That is called **cloning**.

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-hello-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Now move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-hello-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-hello-YOUR_USERNAME
```

Two commands worth knowing, any time you feel lost in the terminal:

- `pwd` — press **Enter** and it tells you which folder you are in.
- `ls` — press **Enter** and it lists what is in that folder.

### Step 4 — Open the project and create your file

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There is no code file yet — you create it yourself.**

For this assignment, create this file:

- `hello.txt`

**To make a file in VS Code:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly — for example `hello.txt` — and press **Enter**.

---

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make a file called `hello.txt` with some words in it.

1. In VS Code, look at the file list down the left-hand side. Hover your mouse over the name of the project at the top of that list — a small row of icons appears.
2. Click the **New File** icon — it looks like a sheet of paper with a `+` on it. *(If you cannot find it, use the menu at the top instead: **File → New File**.)*
3. A box appears for the name. Type exactly:

```
hello.txt
```

and press **Enter**. Spelling matters. All lowercase, one dot, `txt` at the end.

4. The empty file opens in the big area on the right. Click in it and type anything you like — for example:

```
My name is George and this is my first assignment.
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

> The words are up to you. The file must be named `hello.txt` exactly, and it must not be empty.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. Look at the file list on the left of VS Code. `hello.txt` should now be in it.
2. Click on another file in the list, then click back on `hello.txt`. Your words should still be there. That proves it saved.
3. If you would like to see it outside VS Code: **right-click `hello.txt`** → **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. The file is sitting in your assignment folder, like any other file on your computer.

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Your file exists on your computer, but GitHub cannot see it yet. These three commands send it up.

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add hello.txt"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed. The dot means *everything*.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot, with a short note attached so you remember what you did.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

Push often, even when you are only half finished. It costs nothing, and it means your work can never be lost.

### Step 8 — Hand it in

Pushing saves. **Submitting** is different — it asks for your work to be marked. You do that with a **tag**:

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again, and nobody is counting your attempts.

---

**That is the whole routine.** Every assignment from here follows these same nine steps. You only have to learn it once.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | The clone did not finish, or the name is wrong | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is actually there, then `cd` into the name you see |
| Red cross on "created hello.txt" | The file name is wrong | It must be `hello.txt` — all lowercase, no capitals, no space, no `.txt.txt` |
| Red cross on "wrote something in it" | The file is empty, or was never saved | Open it, type some words, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `nothing to commit, working tree clean` | The file was not saved before you ran `git add` | Go to VS Code, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] A file named exactly `hello.txt` exists in the project
- [ ] It has words in it — it is not empty
- [ ] It is saved (no white dot on the VS Code tab)
- [ ] `git push` finished without asking for a password
- [ ] You ran both `git tag submit/1` and `git push origin submit/1`

## Project: load and total a cart safely

The capstone for the whole JavaScript track. You will load a shopping cart that arrives later, total it, and survive anything that goes wrong. This brings together `async` and `await`, `try / catch`, loops, objects, and guard clauses.

You work in `app.js` in your assignment repo.

| Call | Returns |
|---|---|
| `loadTotal(()` | `25` |
| `loadTotal(()` | `12` |
| `loadTotal(()` | `0` |

assignments.name: Change the page text
assignments.description:
## Make JavaScript write on the page **What you are making:** a page whose heading is written by your **JavaScript**, not by your HTML. This is the first time your code changes something a visitor can actually see — until now it has only spoken to the Console. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. - **Your web browser** — Chrome or Edge. You will use a hidden panel inside it called the **Console**. It is one keyboard shortcut away. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-js-dom-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-js-dom-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-js-dom-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There is no code file yet — you create it yourself.** For this assignment, create these files: - `index.html` - `script.js` **To make a file in VS Code:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly — for example `index.html` — and press **Enter**. Do this for each file listed. --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** put a heading on the page, then make your JavaScript rewrite its words. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the heading on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Look near the bottom of the file for the line ``. That line is the end of the part people see. 3. If you can already see a line reading ``, delete that whole line. You are about to type it again, in the place it has to be. 4. Click at the end of the line **above** `` and press **Enter** for a new line. 5. Type this exactly: ```html

Waiting for JavaScript

``` 6. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — find it and change it (in `script.js`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `script.js`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```javascript const title = document.querySelector("#title"); title.textContent = "JavaScript wrote this"; ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What every piece is doing — read this slowly:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `

...

` | A big heading. The `/` in `` marks the closing tag — where the heading ends. | | `id="title"` | A name tag stuck on that heading, so your code can find it. Use an `id` on one element only. | | `` | "Load the file `script.js` and run it." Without this line, nothing in `script.js` ever happens. | | Why that line goes **last** | The browser reads the file from the top down. Your code can only find the heading if the heading has been read already. | | `document` | The page, as JavaScript sees it. | | `.querySelector("#title")` | "Find me the first thing matching `#title`." The `#` means *the element with this id* — in CSS a class took a dot, an id takes a hash. | | `const title = ...` | Keep what was found under the nickname `title`, so the next line can use it. | | `.textContent` | The words inside an element. | | `=` | "Put the thing on the right into the thing on the left." It does not mean "equals". | Each JavaScript line ends with a semicolon `;`. The quotes `" "` wrap words you want treated as plain text. > You may put any words you like inside `"JavaScript wrote this"`, and any words inside the heading. The name `id="title"` in the HTML and `"#title"` in the JavaScript must match exactly, hash and all. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. The heading reads **JavaScript wrote this** — not `Waiting for JavaScript`. The words you typed into the HTML were replaced by your code, in the instant the page loaded. **That is your JavaScript changing the page itself.** Every page you have ever seen update without reloading does exactly this. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Still says `Waiting for JavaScript`? Press the **F12** key. A panel opens at the side or bottom of the browser *(Mac: **Command + Option + J**)*. Click the tab called **Console**, then press **Ctrl + R** to reload with it open. Red text there names the line in `script.js` that went wrong. Keep that panel open while you work — it is where the browser tells you what broke. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Change the heading text with JavaScript" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The heading is still black | The `` line is missing or mistyped | Inside `` it must read exactly `` | | The heading is still black, and the `` line looks right | `style.css` was never saved | Click the `style.css` tab at the top of VS Code and press **Ctrl + S** | | **Every** word on the page turned red | The selector is `body`, not `h1` | Change the first line of the rule to read `h1 {` | | Red cross on "has a CSS rule" | The rule was typed into `index.html` | Rules with `{` and `}` belong in `style.css`. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — make a column to measure (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Type this: ```html

A column that knows its limits

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — write the sizing rules (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. ## Pick a font and open the lines **What you are making:** a page set in a font you chose, with a large title and paragraphs whose lines have room to breathe. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-fonts-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-fonts-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-fonts-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.** CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step) - `style.css` — where you write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** choose a font for the page, make the title bigger, and push the lines of your paragraphs further apart. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — make sure there is a long paragraph (in `index.html`)** Line spacing is the gap between one line of a paragraph and the next. A paragraph only one line long has no gaps to show you, so it needs to be long. 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. What you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this. You may write your own words instead, as long as the paragraph is long enough to wrap onto three or four lines: ```html

Typography

Typography is the choice and the arrangement of the letters on a page, and it decides how willing a person is to read what you wrote. A long paragraph like this one is the only honest way to see line spacing at work, because line spacing is the gap between one line and the next. ``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — write the typography rules (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. It must read `line-height: 1.6;` | | The title did not grow | `font-size` landed in the wrong rule | It must sit inside the `h1 { }` brackets, not `body` or `p` | | Red cross on "sets line-height" | The hyphen is missing, or the file was not saved | The line must read `line-height: 1.6;`. Then click the `style.css` tab and press **Ctrl + S** | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] The `body` rule has `font-family: Georgia, Times, serif;`, ending in a generic fallback - [ ] The `p` rule has `line-height: 1.6;` with no `px` after the number - [ ] The `h1` rule has `font-size: 40px;` - [ ] `index.html` has a paragraph long enough to wrap onto several lines - [ ] Every line inside the brackets ends with `;` and every rule ends with `}` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You can see the wider line spacing in your browser

The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** make three links sit side by side as grey buttons, and make one paragraph disappear from the page completely. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. Now the idea behind this task. Every single thing on a web page is secretly one of two shapes. - A **block** demands a whole line to itself and stretches across the full width available, however few words it holds. Headings, paragraphs and `
` are blocks. Think of a shelf: one item per shelf, and each shelf runs wall to wall. - An **inline** thing sits in the middle of a line of writing and is only as wide as the words in it. Links, `` and `` are inline. Think of a word in a sentence: the next word carries straight on beside it. That is the whole answer to "why is this on its own line?" — because it is a block. `display` is the property that lets you overrule which shape a thing is, and overruling it is this entire task. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the things on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html
Home About Contact

You will never see this sentence.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the shoebox. The three links live inside it. | | `` | One link, and one **child** of that container. There are three of them. | | `href="#"` | Where the link goes. A lone `#` means "nowhere yet — stay on this page". It keeps the link clickable while you have no other pages to point at. | | `class="menu-item"` | The label you will aim at from the CSS. **No dot here.** The dot only appears on the CSS side. | | The two spaces before each `` | Indenting. The computer does not need it. Your eye does — it shows at a glance what is inside the box. | **Half 2 — change the shapes (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Without it you could not see the cushion you have added, because padding itself draws nothing at all. | | `display: none;` | Remove this thing from the page entirely. Not moved, not made see-through — **gone**, and it leaves no gap where it used to be. This is how "show more" panels and pop-ups wait out of sight until they are wanted. | | `.menu-item` and `.secret` | The dot at the front means "everything wearing this label". The names must match the HTML exactly, capital letters included. | `display: none` is worth respecting. If something you wrote has vanished for no reason you can see, a stray `display: none` is the first thing to look for. > You may change the words `Home`, `About` and `Contact`, the sentence in the hidden paragraph, and the colour word `lightgrey` — try `pink` or `lightblue`. The labels `menu-item` and `secret` must stay as they are, and the two lines `display: inline-block;` and `display: none;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. **Home**, **About** and **Contact** now sit side by side in a single row, each one inside its own grey rectangle, with a clear cushion of grey above, below and either side of the word. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. Want to watch `display` do its work? In `style.css`, delete the line `display: inline-block;`, save, and reload the browser. The words stay in their row but the grey rectangles squash flat, because a plain inline link will not grow upwards or downwards. Type the line back in and save again. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Lay out a menu with display" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. **The noticeboard and the drawing pin.** Picture a cork noticeboard on a wall. You can pin a note anywhere on it and describe exactly where: *three centimetres down from the top edge, two centimetres in from the right edge*. Those two measurements only mean anything because you have agreed which board you are measuring from. CSS works in exactly that way, and it takes two lines, one on each thing: - On the **container** you write `position: relative;`. It means: *I am the board. Measure from my edges.* On its own it moves nothing. - On the **child** you write `position: absolute;` and then the measurements. It means: *lift me off the page and stick me here.* Leave out the line on the board and the pin does not fail quietly — it measures from the whole page instead, and lands in the top-right corner of the page, far from your card. That single line is what keeps the label where you want it. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — build the card (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html
New

Mountain bike

A strong bike for rough paths and long hills.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the noticeboard. The label, the heading and the paragraph are all inside it. | | `New` | The **child** you are going to pin. `` is a small box that draws nothing by itself. | | `class="card"` and `class="tag"` | The two labels you will aim at from the CSS. **No dots here.** | | The two spaces before the inner lines | Indenting, so your eye can see what is inside the card. | Look at the page in the browser now if you like. The word **New** sits on a line of its own, above the heading, doing nothing interesting. That is correct so far. **Half 2 — pin the label (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .card { position: relative; width: 300px; padding: 20px; background-color: whitesmoke; } .tag { position: absolute; top: 10px; right: 10px; background-color: crimson; color: white; padding: 4px 8px; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each new line does:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `position: relative;` on `.card` | *I am the board.* It shifts the card not one pixel. Its whole job is to give the children something to measure from. It is the line people forget. | | `position: absolute;` on `.tag` | *Lift me off the page.* The label stops taking up any room of its own — the heading and paragraph now behave as though it were not there — and waits to be told where to go. | | `top: 10px;` | 10 pixels **down** from the top edge of the card. | | `right: 10px;` | 10 pixels **in** from the right edge of the card. `left` and `bottom` exist too, and work the same way from the other sides. | | `width: 300px;` | How wide the card is, so it does not stretch across the whole window and leave the label stranded far to the right. | | `padding: 20px;` | The cushion inside the card, so the heading is not pressed against the edge and the corner is free for the label. | | `color: white;` and `background-color: crimson;` | White words on a red label. | There is a third value worth knowing the name of: `position: fixed;` glues a thing to the browser window itself, so it stays put while the rest of the page scrolls past. That is how a bar stays at the top of a long page. You do not need it here. > The words `Mountain bike`, the sentence, the label word `New` and the two colours are all yours to change. The labels `card` and `tag` must stay as they are, and the four lines `position: relative;`, `position: absolute;`, `top: 10px;` and `right: 10px;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. A pale grey card about as wide as a playing card is tall, holding the heading *Mountain bike* and a sentence below it. 5. In the **top-right corner of that grey card**, lying on top of it, a small red label reading **New** with white letters. 6. Notice what has moved. Before you wrote the CSS, the word *New* sat on a line of its own **above** the heading and pushed the heading down the page. Now it is up in the corner, and the heading has risen to the top of the card to take the space back. The label is occupying no room of its own at all — it is floating over the card. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. The label is in the corner of the **page** instead of the corner of the card? That is the missing line: `.card` needs `position: relative;`. Without it the label measured from the whole page. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Pin a tag to a card corner" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The word **New** is in the top-right corner of the whole page, nowhere near the card | `.card` is missing `position: relative;`, so the label measured from the page | Add `position: relative;` as the first line inside the `.card { }` rule and save | | The word **New** still sits on its own line above the heading | `.tag` is missing `position: absolute;`, or the `` has no `class="tag"` | Check for `position: absolute;` in the `.tag` rule, and `class="tag"` in `index.html` | | The label is in the top-**left** corner of the card | You wrote `left: 10px;` where the instructions say `right: 10px;` | Change the word `left` to `right` and save | | The label is sitting on top of the heading's words | The card has no padding, so there is no empty corner for the label to sit in | Check the `.card` rule contains `padding: 20px;` | | Red cross on "uses an offset" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed, so `top:` and `right:` never reached GitHub | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains `position: relative;` inside the `.card` rule - [ ] `style.css` contains `position: absolute;` inside the `.tag` rule - [ ] `style.css` contains both `top: 10px;` and `right: 10px;` - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` with a `` inside it - [ ] Every rule ends with `}` and every line inside it ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] In the browser: the red **New** label sits in the card's own top-right corner
