assignments.description:
## Wrap words around a photograph **What you are making:** a page where a photograph sits against the left edge and the words of a paragraph run around its right-hand side, the way a picture sits in a newspaper column. **Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-float-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-float-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-float-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.** CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step) - `style.css` — where you write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** push a photograph to the left edge of the page and let a paragraph's words flow around its right-hand side. **The stone in the stream.** Picture a stream of water running down the page. The water is your words. Drop a stone into the stream and the water does not stop — it parts, runs around the stone, and closes up again below it. `float` is how you drop the stone. `float: left;` shoves it against the left bank; `float: right;` shoves it against the right. Everything written after it flows around the gap. This is float's one genuinely good job today. Older websites also used it to build whole columns of a page — you will meet far better tools for that shortly, so use `float` for pictures and leave it there. You will still recognise it in older code, which is the other reason to know it. This has two halves. Do them in order. The first half is longer than usual, because you need a photograph before you can float one. **Half 1 — get a photograph onto the page (in `index.html`)** A picture only appears if the picture file is sitting **next to** `index.html`, in the same folder. So the first job is putting a file in the right place. 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list on the left, then click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. A window opens showing your assignment folder. **Leave this window open** — this is where the photograph must land. 2. Open your web browser and go to `https://unsplash.com`. 3. Click any photograph you like. It opens larger. 4. **Right-click** on the large photograph, then click **Save image as…**. A save window appears. 5. In that save window, find the box labelled **File name**. Delete what is in it and type `photo.jpg` — all small letters, ending in `.jpg`. 6. Still in that save window, on the left-hand side click **Documents**, then double-click the folder **`lacefi-academy`**, then double-click the folder whose name begins `webdev-css-float-`. Click **Save**. 7. Look back at the File Explorer window from action 1. `photo.jpg` should now be sitting beside `index.html`. If it is not there, it went somewhere else — see the table at the bottom of this page. 8. Go back to VS Code. `photo.jpg` now appears in the file list on the left. In that list, **click once on `index.html`**. 9. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Click at the end of a line between them, press **Enter**, and type this exactly: ```html

I am learning to build web pages. This week I found out that a picture does not have to sit on a line of its own with empty space either side of it. It can be pushed hard against one edge, and the writing can be allowed to run around it, which is how newspapers and magazines have set their pages for two hundred years. The instruction has a name in CSS, and the name is float. It takes two lines to write and it changes the whole feel of a page. I am going to keep writing for a few sentences longer, so that there are enough words here to run down past the bottom of the photograph and back out to the full width of the page, because that is the part that makes the effect obvious.

``` 10. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `` | The tag for a picture. It is a lonely tag — there is **no** ``. | | `src="photo.jpg"` | The **source**: the name of the picture file, spelled exactly as it appears in the VS Code file list, `.jpg` included. | | `alt="…"` | A short honest description in words. It is read aloud to people who cannot see, and it appears if the picture fails to load. Change it to describe the photograph you actually chose. | | `class="photo"` and `class="story"` | The two labels you will aim at from the CSS. **No dots here.** | The paragraph is deliberately long. A short paragraph would not have enough words to reach the bottom of the picture, and you would not see the effect at all. **Half 2 — drop the stone in the stream (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .photo { float: left; width: 200px; margin-right: 20px; margin-bottom: 10px; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each line does:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `float: left;` | The stone. Push the photograph hard against the left edge and let the words run round its right-hand side. | | `width: 200px;` | Photographs from the internet are enormous — often wider than your whole screen. This shrinks it to 200 pixels across so there is room for words beside it. You do not set a height; the picture keeps its own proportions on its own. | | `margin-right: 20px;` | A 20-pixel gap **outside** the photograph, on its right. Without it the words press against the edge of the picture and the page looks cramped. | | `margin-bottom: 10px;` | The same gap underneath, so the line of words that wraps below the picture does not touch it either. | One thing to know for later. A floated thing is lifted out of the normal flow, so the container holding it can collapse to nothing, and things written after it can slide up beside it when you did not want them to. The cure is `clear: both;` on whatever should start below the float. You do not need it in this task. > Choose any photograph you like, and write your own paragraph if you prefer — keep it long, at least six or seven lines on screen, or there will not be enough words to wrap. The picture file must be named `photo.jpg`, the labels must stay `photo` and `story`, and the line `float: left;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Your photograph now sits hard against the **left-hand edge** of the page, about 200 pixels across — roughly a quarter of the window. 5. The paragraph no longer begins underneath it. Its first several lines now start **to the right of the photograph**, each line beginning a clear gap away from the picture's edge. 6. Follow the words down with your eye. The moment they pass the **bottom** of the photograph they swing back out to the full width of the page. That step in the left-hand margin is the whole effect. Before you wrote the CSS the photograph filled the page at its own enormous size and every word of the paragraph sat below it. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. A small broken-picture symbol and your `alt` words instead of a photograph? The file is not beside `index.html`, or it is not named `photo.jpg`. Look at the VS Code file list on the left: `photo.jpg` must be in it. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Float an image and wrap the text" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | A small broken-picture symbol instead of a photograph | `photo.jpg` is not in the assignment folder, or the name is spelled differently | Check the VS Code file list on the left. If `photo.jpg` is not listed, save the photograph again into the folder whose name begins `webdev-css-float-` | | The photograph fills the page and no words sit beside it | The `width: 200px;` line is missing, so the picture is at its full size | Add `width: 200px;` inside the `.photo { }` rule and save | | The words are touching the edge of the photograph | The `margin-right` line is missing | Add `margin-right: 20px;` inside the `.photo { }` rule and save | | The photograph is on its own line with all the words below it | The `` tag has no `class="photo"`, so the rule never finds it | The tag must begin `` tag carries `class="photo"` — no dot - [ ] The paragraph is long enough to run past the bottom of the photograph - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] In the browser: the words wrap around the right-hand side of the picture

## Give a box its own scrollbar **What you are making:** a small box holding more words than it can fit, which grows a little scrollbar of its own instead of spilling down the page — and two overlapping coloured squares where you decide which one is in front. **Time:** about 40 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-overflow-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-overflow-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-overflow-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.** CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step) - `style.css` — where you write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** two things. Make a small box keep its size and scroll its own contents. Then make two overlapping squares swap over, so the one that would be underneath comes to the front. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. **The envelope.** Picture an envelope with room for three sheets of paper. Push in six and the extra sheets stick out of the top for everyone to see. That is what a web page does by default when the words are taller than the box meant to hold them: they spill out and carry on down the page. `overflow` is the instruction that changes this. `overflow: auto;` says: keep everything inside the envelope, and give me a small handle down the side so I can slide the papers up and down. **The desk.** Now picture sheets of paper laid on a desk, overlapping. Whichever you put down last covers the ones already there. A web page does exactly the same: things written later cover things written earlier. `z-index` lets you number the sheets instead of relying on the order you dropped them. The **higher** the number, the nearer it is to your eyes. One catch, and it catches everybody: **`z-index` is ignored unless the thing also has a `position`.** A plain box cannot be reordered. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — build the box and the squares (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Everything you add goes **between those two lines**. 3. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter** to make a new line. 4. Type this exactly: ```html

Monday. I made a heading and a paragraph and they both appeared in the browser, which still feels like a small miracle.

Tuesday. I learned that padding is the space inside a box and margin is the space outside it.

Wednesday. I put three links in a row and hid a paragraph with display none.

Thursday. I pinned a label to the corner of a card with position absolute.

Friday. Today I am giving a box a scrollbar of its very own.

Front
Back
``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container** — the envelope. The five diary paragraphs are its **children**. | | `
` … `
` | A second container, holding the two squares. | | `class="front"` and `class="back"` | The two squares. Read the order carefully: **`front` is written first, `back` is written second.** | That order is not an accident. Left alone, the page would put `back` on top, because things written later cover things written earlier. Your `z-index` is going to overrule that — which is exactly how you will be able to see it working. **Half 2 — control the spill and the stack (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css .notes { width: 300px; height: 140px; padding: 10px; background-color: whitesmoke; overflow: auto; } .stack { position: relative; height: 180px; } .front { position: absolute; top: 20px; left: 20px; width: 120px; height: 120px; background-color: crimson; z-index: 2; } .back { position: absolute; top: 60px; left: 60px; width: 120px; height: 120px; background-color: royalblue; z-index: 1; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each new line does:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `height: 140px;` on `.notes` | The size of the envelope. **This is the line that creates the problem `overflow` solves.** Without a fixed height the box would grow to fit the words and nothing would ever spill. | | `overflow: auto;` | Keep what does not fit inside the box, and add a scrollbar only if one is needed. | | `position: relative;` on `.stack` | *I am the board.* The two squares measure from this container's edges. | | `height: 180px;` on `.stack` | An absolutely placed child takes up no room, so this container would otherwise collapse to nothing and the squares would lie on top of whatever came next. The height holds the space open. | | `top` and `left` on the squares | How far down and how far in each square starts. The second square starts 40 pixels further down and across, which is what makes them overlap. | | `z-index: 2;` and `z-index: 1;` | The layer numbers. 2 is nearer your eyes than 1, so the red square wins — even though it is written first in the HTML. | `overflow` has four values worth knowing: - `visible` — the default. The extra spills out of the box and everyone sees it. - `hidden` — chop off whatever does not fit. It is still there, but nobody can reach it. - `scroll` — always show a scrollbar, even when everything fits. - `auto` — show a scrollbar **only when one is needed**. This is nearly always the one you want, and the one you have written. > The diary sentences and the two colours are yours to change, and you may adjust the `height` of `.notes` — but keep it small enough that the words do not fit, or there will be no scrollbar to see. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Near the top of the page, a small pale grey box about as wide as a postcard, showing only the first two or three lines of your diary. Down its right-hand edge there is now a **thin scrollbar**. Rest your mouse over the grey box and roll the wheel: the diary slides up and down **inside** the box while the rest of the page stays perfectly still. Before you wrote the CSS, all five diary lines ran straight down the page, with no box and no scrollbar anywhere. 5. Below the grey box, two squares overlapping like two beer mats pushed together. The **red** one is in front, whole and unbroken. The **blue** one is behind it, down and to the right, with only its lower-right corner showing. 6. That is the opposite of what the page would do on its own, because `back` is written **after** `front` in your HTML. The `z-index` numbers are what brought the red square forward. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. Want proof the `z-index` is doing the work? In `style.css`, change `z-index: 2;` to `z-index: 0;`, save, and reload. The blue square jumps in front of the red one. Change it back to `2` and save again. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add overflow scrolling and a z-index" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The diary runs down the whole page and there is no scrollbar | The `.notes` rule has no `height`, so the box grew to fit the words instead of the words being made to fit the box | Check the `.notes` rule contains `height: 140px;` | | The last diary lines are chopped off and there is no scrollbar | You typed `overflow: hidden;` instead of `overflow: auto;` | Change the word `hidden` to `auto` and save | | The blue square is in front of the red one | The `z-index` numbers are missing, or they are the wrong way round | `.front` must have the **higher** number: `z-index: 2;` on `.front`, `z-index: 1;` on `.back` | | The two squares sit one below the other and never overlap | `position: absolute;` is missing from one of them, or `.stack` has no `position: relative;` | Both `.front` and `.back` need `position: absolute;`, and `.stack` needs `position: relative;` | | Red cross on "uses overflow" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - assignments.description:
## Build the bar across the top **What you are making:** a dark strip across the top of your page holding three links — **Home**, **About** and **Contact** — evenly spaced, with the underlines taken off, that light up when your mouse rests on them. Every website you have ever used has one of these. **Time:** about 35 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-navbar-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-navbar-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-navbar-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.** CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step) - `style.css` — where you write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** build the row of links that sits across the top of every website, and make it light up under the mouse. Think of the top of almost any website you have visited: a strip of colour with a handful of words in a row, and each word brightening as the mouse passes over it. That strip is called a **navigation bar**, or **navbar** for short. You are about to build one, and from now on you will notice them everywhere. Two words first. They run through the whole of this module, so it is worth thirty seconds now. A **container** is a box that holds other things. Picture a shoebox on a shelf. In HTML, anything you write between a tag's opening line and its closing line is **inside** that box. The things inside are its **children**. The shoebox is the container; the shoes are its children. When an instruction says "put this rule on the container", it means the outer box. When it says "the children sit in a row", it means the things inside it. A navbar is nothing more than a container holding some links as its children — the shoebox and the shoes. Three pieces of CSS turn that into a bar: - one line on the **container** that lays its children out in a row, - a few lines on the **children** to smarten them up, - and one small rule that only fires while the mouse is resting on a link. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — the three links (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the **end** of that line and press **Enter** to make a new line directly beneath it. The bar must be the **first** thing inside the body, so that it sits across the top of the page. 3. Type this exactly: ```html
Home About Contact
``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **What you have written:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `
` … `
` | The **container**. It is a box like `
`, but its name tells anybody reading the page — including the software that reads pages aloud to blind people — that these links are the site's main navigation. | | `class="navbar"` | The label you will aim at from the CSS. **No dot here.** | | `Home` | One link, and one **child** of the container. | | `href="#"` | Where the link goes. A lone `#` means "nowhere yet — stay on this page". It keeps the link clickable while you have no other pages to point at. | **Half 2 — turn them into a bar (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. It is three separate rules — leave the blank lines in, they make it easier to read: ```css .navbar { display: flex; gap: 20px; background-color: #222222; padding: 14px 24px; } .navbar a { color: white; text-decoration: none; padding: 8px 12px; border-radius: 6px; } .navbar a:hover { background-color: #444444; } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **The three rules, one at a time.** The first rule is aimed at the **container**: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: flex;` | Said to the container, this means: take your children and lay them out in a row, and let me control the spacing between them. There is a whole lesson on flex ahead; for today this one line is all you need. | | `gap: 20px;` | The space **between** the children — 20 pixels between each link and the next. You write it once on the container instead of putting a margin on every child. | | `background-color: #222222;` | The colour of the bar. A colour written as a code rather than a name: this one is a very dark grey, close to black. Colour names like `white` work here too. | | `padding: 14px 24px;` | The cushion inside the bar: 14 pixels above and below the links, 24 pixels at each end. This is what gives the bar its height. | The second rule is aimed at the **children**, and its name is the important part: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `.navbar a` | Two names with a **space** between them. In CSS, a space means **inside**. This rule finds every `` that lives inside something wearing the `navbar` label, and leaves every other link on your page completely alone. | | `color: white;` | The words themselves — white letters on the dark bar. | | `text-decoration: none;` | Takes the underline off. Links come underlined by default; in a bar the underline looks wrong, and the bar itself already makes it plain they are clickable. | | `padding: 8px 12px;` | A cushion inside each link, so the highlight has room to appear around the word and the link is comfortable to click. | | `border-radius: 6px;` | Rounds the corners of that highlight. | The third rule is aimed at a **state**: | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `:hover` | Not a thing but a moment — it means "while the mouse is resting on this". The rule switches on the instant the pointer arrives and switches off the instant it leaves. | | `a:hover` | Note there is **no space** before the colon. `a:hover` means the link while hovered. `a :hover` — with a space — means something else entirely and will not work. | > The three words may be anything you like — `Shop`, `Blog`, `About me`. The two colours are yours as well. The label must stay `navbar`, and the lines `display: flex;` and `text-decoration: none;` and the rule ending `:hover` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. Across the **top** of your page there is now a strip of very dark grey, running the full width of the window. Sitting inside it, in a row starting from the left, the three words **Home**, **About** and **Contact** in white letters, with a clear gap between one and the next, and no underlines anywhere. 5. Everything else on your page has been pushed down to begin below the bar. Before you wrote the CSS, those three words were blue, underlined, and running together on one plain line with a single space between them and nothing behind them. 6. Now move your mouse slowly onto the word **About** and rest it there without clicking. A lighter grey rectangle with rounded corners appears behind that word alone, and vanishes the moment you move the mouse away. Try all three in turn. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Nothing changed at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `` for a line reading ``. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Build a navigation bar" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The three words are stacked one above the other | `display: flex;` is missing or misspelled, so the container is not laying its children in a row | Check the `.navbar` rule contains `display: flex;` exactly, with the colon and the semicolon | | The links are still blue and underlined, and the bar has no words on it | The `.navbar a` rule is not reaching them — most often the space between the two names is missing | It must read `.navbar a {` with exactly one space. `.navbara` is a different name entirely | | Nothing happens when the mouse rests on a link | There is a space before the colon, or the rule is aimed at the bar instead of the links | It must read `.navbar a:hover {` — no space before the colon | | The bar is dark but the words cannot be seen | The words are still their default dark colour on a nearly black bar | Check the `.navbar a` rule contains `color: white;` | | Red cross on "uses flex" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `display: flex;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a line reading `text-decoration: none;` - [ ] `style.css` contains a rule whose name ends `:hover` — with no space before the colon - [ ] `.navbar a` is written with exactly one space between the two names - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` with three `` links inside it - [ ] Every rule ends with `}` and every line inside it ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Before any code, one idea. The rest of this module rests on it, so read it twice. **The tray and the cups** Picture a tray with three cups standing on it. - The **tray** is the thing that holds. Now suppose you want the cups arranged in a neat row, spread to the edges of the tray. You do not walk up to each cup and give it an instruction. You give one instruction to the **tray**: *hold your cups in a row, spread out*. The tray arranges them. CSS works exactly this way. The instruction `display: flex` goes on the **container** — the tray. The children move because of it. You never put `display: flex` on a cup. In this task one big `
` holds three smaller `
` boxes. The big one is the tray. The three small ones are the cups. You style the tray, and the cups line up. **Half 1 — build the tray and the cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that says ``. Logo
Home
About
``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | The outer `
` … `

` normally takes a whole line to itself, so right now these three words sit one under the other. That is what you are about to change. | | The two spaces starting each inner line | Indentation. ` and `
`. That is what makes them children of the tray. Save and look at the page now if you like: three words, stacked one per line. Without `display: flex` each word would have been on a line of its own, one under the other. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Still stacked one per line? The `display: flex;` line is missing, misspelled, or sitting in a rule other than `.menu`. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. ` is the **tray**. Each `
` inside it is a **cup**. The difference this time: you give instructions to both. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Card one
Card two
Card three
Card four
``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `class="cards"` | The label on the tray. Note the **s** on the end. | | `class="card"` | The label on each cup. No **s**. These are two different labels, and one letter apart, so type carefully. | | Four `
` boxes with the same label | A label may be worn by as many things as you like. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The cards are stacked one per line at any window width | `display: flex` is missing, or it landed in the `.card` rule | It belongs in `.cards` — the rule for the tray, spelled with an **s** | | The cards squash into thin slivers instead of dropping to a new line | `flex-wrap: wrap;` is missing | Add it inside the `.cards` rule, on its own line ending with a semicolon | | The cards touch each other with no space between | `gap: 16px;` is missing or was typed in the `.card` rule | `gap` only works on the tray — move it into `.cards` | | The cards are all different widths and do not fill the row | `flex: 1 1 250px;` is missing from the `.card` rule | Add it as the first line inside `.card`. Three values, separated by single spaces | | Red cross on "uses flex-wrap or flex" | `style.css` was not saved before you pushed | Click the `style.css` tab, press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` holding four `
` boxes - [ ] `style.css` has a rule starting `.cards {` containing `display: flex;` - [ ] That same rule contains `flex-wrap: wrap;` and `gap: 16px;` - [ ] A separate rule starting `.card {` contains `flex: 1 1 250px;` - [ ] Both rules are closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] Narrowing the browser window makes the cards wrap onto a second line

` is the **tray**; the six boxes inside are the **cups**, and you arrange them by instructing the tray. What is new is which tray you use. Flexbox arranges children along **one** line — a row. **Grid** arranges them in rows and columns **at the same time**, like eggs in an egg box. Galleries and photo walls are grid work. **Half 1 — build the tray and six cups (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line under it. 3. Type this: ```html
Box one
Box two
Box three
Box four

``` All six boxes sit between `

`. Only children of the tray get placed in the grid. 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. **Half 2 — describe the grid (in `style.css`)** 1. Type this exactly, all four rules, in this order: ```css .layout { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr); gap: 16px; } .box { padding: 20px; background-color: #fde68a; border-radius: 8px; text-align: center; } .header { grid-column: span 4; } .feature { grid-column: span 2; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `repeat(4, 1fr)` | Four columns, each one equal share wide. The `4` is a count; the comma separates it from the width. | | `grid-column: span 4;` | This cup covers **4** columns instead of 1. On a four-column grid, that is the full width. | | `grid-column: span 2;` | This cup covers **2** columns — twice as wide as an ordinary one. | | `span` | The word is part of the instruction here. It has nothing to do with the `` tag. | | Why `.header` comes after `.box` | Both rules apply to the header box. They set different things, so they do not argue; the box gets its padding and colour from one and its width from the other. | 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > You may change the wording inside the boxes, the colour code and the padding. You may also give one box `grid-row: span 2;` to make it two rows tall. Keep `display: grid;`, keep `repeat(4, 1fr)`, and keep at least one `grid-column:` line — the checker looks for a `grid-column` or `grid-row` instruction. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see three rows of yellow boxes: - **Row one:** the box marked *Header*, stretched across the **full width** of the page on its own. - **Row two:** *Feature* on the left, **twice as wide** as the boxes beside it, then *One* and *Two*. - **Row three:** *Three*, *Four* and *Five*, each one column wide, with an empty space where a fourth would go. 5. All the gaps between boxes are even, and every box has the same yellow fill and rounded corners. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Every box the same width? The `grid-column` lines are not landing — check the two-label spelling `class="box header"` in the HTML against `.header` in the CSS. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Span grid items across columns" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | *Header* sits in one column like all the others | The `header` label is missing or misspelled in one of the two files | The HTML needs `class="box header"` (one space, no dot) and the CSS needs `.header {` (with a dot) | | *Header* stretches across, but has no yellow fill or padding | The word `box` was left off that `
` | It must carry both labels: `class="box header"` | | All seven boxes sit in one tall column | `display: grid;` or the `grid-template-columns` line is missing from `.layout` | Both belong inside the `.layout` rule, each ending with a semicolon | | There are more or fewer than four columns | The number in `repeat(4, 1fr)` was mistyped | It reads `repeat(4, 1fr)` — a `4`, a comma, then `1fr`, with one closing bracket | | Red cross on "spans an item" | The property was typed without its hyphen, or `style.css` was not saved | It is `grid-column`, not `gridcolumn`. Then press **Ctrl + S** and repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` holding seven boxes - [ ] One box carries `class="box header"` and one carries `class="box feature"` - [ ] `style.css` has `.layout {` containing `display: grid;` and `grid-template-columns: repeat(4, 1fr);` - [ ] There is a `.header` rule containing `grid-column: span 4;` - [ ] There is a `.feature` rule containing `grid-column: span 2;` - [ ] Every rule is closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

assignments.description: ## Build a card gallery that reflows **What you are making:** a finished gallery page — a heading and four cards, each with a coloured top strip, a title and a line of text — laid out in a grid that changes how many cards it puts per row as the window changes size. This is the layout real shop and portfolio sites use. **Time:** about 45 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-layout-project-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-layout-project-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-layout-project-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you make them yourself**, then paste the starter below into `index.html`. CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page - `style.css` — where you will write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, **paste in exactly this**, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My Page ``` This is the **starter skeleton**: the `` holds information about the page, and the `` holds everything people see. Leave `style.css` empty for now — you connect it and write your CSS in the next step. *Tip: in an empty `.html` file you can also type a single `!` and press **Tab**, and VS Code writes this skeleton for you — the shortcut is called Emmet. Pasting the block above is the sure route, since it already includes this lesson's exact starting point.* --- ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** build a complete page — a heading and four cards in a grid — that rearranges itself as the window changes width. This one is longer than the others in this module, so it is split into six stages. Do them in order and save as you go. Nothing here is new: it is the tray and the cups, the grid, and the card styling you have already met, put together into one page. --- **Half 1 — build the page (in `index.html`)** **Stage 1 — connect your two files** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. 2. Look near the top of the file, between `` and ``, for a line that reads: ```html ``` 3. If that line is already there, change nothing and go to Stage 2. If it is not there, click at the end of the `` line, press **Enter**, and type it in. That single line is what makes `style.css` affect this page. Without it your styling is written but never used, and the checker will mark it as missing. **Stage 2 — clear the old content out of the body** 1. Find the line that says `<body>` and the line that says `</body>`. 2. Click at the very start of the first line **below** `<body>`, hold the **Shift** key down, and click at the very end of the last line **above** `</body>`. Everything between turns blue. 3. Press **Backspace** *(the key above Enter, sometimes marked ←)*. 4. Leave `<body>` and `</body>` themselves alone. If you deleted one by accident, type it back. **Stage 3 — type the heading and the four cards** 1. Put the blinking line between `<body>` and `</body>`. 2. Type this. It is repetitive on purpose — the four cards are identical apart from their words: ```html <h1>My Gallery</h1> <div class="gallery"> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>First card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Second card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Third card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> <div class="card"> <div class="card-top"></div> <h2>Fourth card</h2> <p>A short line about this card.</p> </div> </div> ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `<div class="gallery">` | The tray. It holds the four cards. | | `<div class="card">` | One cup — and itself a small tray, because it holds three things of its own. Trays inside trays is ordinary and expected. | | `<div class="card-top"></div>` | An opening tag and a closing tag with **nothing between them**: an empty box. It exists only so you can give it a height and a colour and get a coloured strip. | | The hyphen in `card-top` | Part of the name. A label may contain hyphens; it may not contain spaces. | 3. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. --- **Half 2 — style the page (in `style.css`)** In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. Stages 4, 5 and 6 are typed one after another, down the same file. **Stage 4 — settle the page itself** 1. Type this: ```css * { box-sizing: border-box; } body { font-family: Arial, sans-serif; background-color: #f4f4f4; padding: 20px; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `*` | A star means **every single thing on the page**. No dot, no name. | | `box-sizing: border-box;` | Tells the browser to count padding and borders **inside** a box's stated width, not on top of it. Without it, widths creep past what you asked for. Put this line in every project. | | `font-family: Arial, sans-serif;` | Use Arial; if the computer has no Arial, use any plain typeface. The comma offers an alternative. | | `padding: 20px;` | A cushion round the whole page, so nothing touches the window edge. | **Stage 5 — make the gallery a responsive grid** 1. Press **Enter** twice to leave a blank line, then type this: ```css .gallery { display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(200px, 1fr)); gap: 16px; } ``` This is the same recipe you used for the box gallery: *as many columns as fit, each at least 200 pixels wide, sharing the leftover space equally*, with 16 pixels of space between every row and column. Count the closing brackets: `1fr));`. **Stage 6 — style the cards** 1. Press **Enter** twice again, then type this: ```css .card { background-color: white; border: 1px solid #dddddd; border-radius: 8px; padding: 20px; } .card-top { height: 60px; border-radius: 4px; background-color: #60a5fa; margin-bottom: 12px; } ``` | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `border: 1px solid #dddddd;` | Three values in one line, separated by spaces: how thick, what kind of line, what colour. | | `border-radius: 8px;` | Rounds the corners of the card. | | `padding: 20px;` | Space inside the card, between its edge and its contents. | | `height: 60px;` | Forces the empty top box to be 60 pixels tall. An empty box with no height is invisible, which is why this line matters. | | `margin-bottom: 12px;` | Space **outside** the top strip, below it — pushing the title down. Padding is inside a box; margin is outside it. | 2. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. > Change the heading, the card titles and the sentences to whatever you like, and pick your own colour codes. If you would like to go further, add `box-shadow: 0 2px 6px #cccccc;` inside the `.card` rule for a soft shadow. Four things must stay: the `<link>` line in `index.html`, `display: grid;`, the `gap:` line, and the `padding`, `border` and `background-color` lines on `.card`. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. At the top, **My Gallery** in large letters. Below it, four white cards on a light grey page. Each card has a **blue strip across its top**, a title underneath, and a line of text below that. The cards have thin grey borders and rounded corners, with even gaps between them. 5. On a wide window all four cards sit **side by side in one row**, all the same width. On a narrower window some of them will already have dropped onto a second line — that is the layout working, not a fault. 6. Drag the right-hand edge of the browser window slowly to the left. The cards reflow on their own: four across, then three, then two, then a single column stacked one above the other. Drag it back and they climb into a row again. No extra code makes that happen — it is the `minmax(200px, 1fr)` line doing the work. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. Plain black text on a white page, no cards? `style.css` is not connected. Open `index.html` and check for `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` between `<head>` and `</head>`. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Build the card gallery layout" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | Plain text on a white page, no cards and no colour | The `<link>` line is missing from `<head>` | Add `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` between `<head>` and `</head>`, then save and reload | | The cards are styled but stacked in one column on a wide window | `display: grid;` or the `grid-template-columns` line is missing from `.gallery` | Both belong inside `.gallery`, and the long line must end `1fr));` | | The cards have no blue strip at the top | `height: 60px;` is missing from `.card-top` | An empty box with no height cannot be seen. Add the height line and save | | The cards sit flush against each other with no space | `gap: 16px;` is missing | Add it inside the `.gallery` rule — `gap` works on the tray, not the cards | | Red cross on "styles the cards" | The `.card` rule is empty, misspelled, or `style.css` was not saved | The rule needs `padding`, `border` and `background-color` lines. Then press **Ctrl + S** and repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `index.html` has `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">` inside `<head>` - [ ] `index.html` has a `<div class="gallery">` holding four `<div class="card">` boxes - [ ] `style.css` has a rule starting `.gallery {` containing `display: grid;` - [ ] That rule also contains `gap: 16px;` - [ ] There is a `.card` rule with `padding`, `border` and `background-color` lines - [ ] Every rule is closed with `}` and every line inside ends with `;` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)

The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** style three things that plain CSS cannot reach — a button *while* the mouse is over it, a typing box *while* it is selected, and a star that CSS adds for you. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the three things on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that reads ``. It is near the bottom. 3. Click at the end of the line **above** `` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line. 4. Type these three lines exactly: ```html

New

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. A note on the middle line: `` is one of the few tags with **no closing tag**. There is no ``. It is finished the moment you type the `>`. **Half 2 — style them in their special states (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. ## Store a colour once, use it everywhere

**What you are making:** a page whose colour and spacing are written down in **one** place at the top of your CSS. Change that one line and the whole page changes at once.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-variables-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-variables-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-css-variables-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.**

CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files:

- `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step)
- `style.css` — where you write your CSS

**To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file.

Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <title>My page</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
```

The `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `<body>` and `</body>` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`.

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** write a colour and a spacing size once, give each a name, then use those names in two different rules.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — add a button to style (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that reads `</body>`. It is near the bottom.
3. Click at the end of the line **above** `</body>` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line.
4. Type this exactly:

```html
<button class="brand-button">Get in touch</button>
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

**Half 2 — write the names, then use them (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```css
:root {
  --brand: #6a11cb;
  --space: 16px;
}

body {
  color: var(--brand);
  padding: var(--space);
}

.brand-button {
  background-color: var(--brand);
  color: white;
  border: none;
  padding: var(--space);
  font-size: 16px;
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**The new pieces:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `:root` | Stands for the whole page. Names written here can be used by every rule in the file. |
| `--brand` | A name **you** invented. Any name you like, so long as it starts with **two dashes**. The two dashes are what tell CSS "this is a stored value, not a real property". |
| `--brand: #6a11cb;` | Stores the colour under that name. On its own it changes nothing on screen. |
| `var(--brand)` | Fetches the stored value back out. Wherever you write this, CSS puts `#6a11cb`. |
| `#6a11cb` | A colour written as a code: a `#` and six characters. This one is purple. |
| `16px` | Sixteen pixels — a length. A pixel is one dot on your screen. |
| `padding` | Empty breathing space **inside** the edge of the thing. |

The point is not that it looks nice. The point is that the purple now lives in **one** line. You will prove that in Step 6.

> You may use any colour code you like after `--brand:`, and any size after `--space:`. The names `--brand`, `--space` and the `var(...)` wrapping must stay exactly as written.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. All of the writing on the page should now be purple, the page should have a band of empty space round its edge, and the `Get in touch` button should be a solid purple block with white writing on it.

Now prove why variables are worth having:

5. Go back to VS Code, click the `style.css` tab, and change the one line `--brand: #6a11cb;` to read `--brand: #b3261e;` instead.
6. Press **Ctrl + S** to save, click back to the browser, and press **Ctrl + R** to reload.
7. The writing **and** the button turn red together. You changed one line and two rules followed. That is the whole point. Leave it red or put the purple back — either passes.

Nothing is coloured at all? Open `index.html` and look inside `<head>` for a line reading `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css">`. That line is what connects your two files — without it, the CSS is ignored.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add CSS variables for colour and space"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| Nothing is purple, everything looks plain | The name is spelled differently in the two places | `--brand` in `:root` and `var(--brand)` must match letter for letter, including the two dashes |
| Nothing is purple, everything looks plain | One dash instead of two | It must be `--brand`, not `-brand`. Two dashes at the front, both times |
| Red cross on "uses var()" | The `var(` wrapper is missing | `color: --brand;` does not work. It must read `color: var(--brand);` |
| Red cross on "defines a variable" | The `:root` block is missing or has no colon | `:root` needs a line inside it shaped like `--brand: #6a11cb;` — name, colon, value, semicolon |
| The button is purple but the writing is not | The `body` rule was left out | Both rules are needed. The check wants `var(--` used, and the point of the task is using it more than once |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `style.css` has a `:root` block containing `--brand: #6a11cb;` and `--space: 16px;`
- [ ] Each stored name starts with **two** dashes
- [ ] `var(--brand)` is used in at least two different rules
- [ ] `index.html` has the `<button class="brand-button">` line
- [ ] Every line inside the curly brackets ends with `;`
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] Changing the one `--brand` line changes both the writing and the button

Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** make a banner whose background fades from one colour to another. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the banner on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that reads ``. It is near the top. 3. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** to make a new empty line directly underneath it. 4. Type this exactly: ```html
Welcome to my page
``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. A `
` is a plain box with no meaning and no look of its own. It exists so you have something to paint. **Half 2 — paint the blend (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3.
