Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Add a gradient banner" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The banner is there but it is one flat colour | A comma is missing | There must be a comma after the direction and a comma between the two colours: `(to right, #6a11cb, #2575fc)` | | The banner is there but has no background at all | A round bracket is missing | The line needs both: one after `linear-gradient` and one before the `;` | | Red cross on "uses a gradient" | The word is misspelled or split | It is one word with a dash: `linear-gradient`. No space around the dash | | No banner anywhere on the page | The `
` line is missing or is outside `` | It must sit between `` and ``, and read `
Welcome to my page
` | | The banner is a thin strip with the words squashed in | The `padding` line is missing | `padding: 40px;` is what gives the band its height | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains `background: linear-gradient(` followed by a direction and two colours - [ ] There is a comma after the direction and a comma between the two colours - [ ] The round bracket opened after `linear-gradient` is closed before the `;` - [ ] `index.html` has a `
` between `` and `` - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You can see the colours fading into each other in your browser

## Make a card float off the page **What you are making:** a white card with a soft shadow underneath it, so it looks as though it is sitting slightly above the page — and the shadow grows when you point at it, as if the card rises to meet your hand. **Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. Do this once for each file. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** give a box a soft shadow, then a bigger shadow while the mouse is over it. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — put the card on the page (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Find the line that reads ``. It is near the bottom. 3. Click at the end of the line **above** `` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line. 4. Type these four lines exactly. The two middle lines are indented by two spaces — press the **space bar** twice at the start of each: ```html

My first card

This box lifts when you point at it.

``` 5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. The indenting changes nothing on screen. It is there so you can see at a glance that the heading and the paragraph live **inside** the card. **Half 2 — give it a shadow (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly: ```css body { background-color: #f4f4f4; } .card { background-color: white; width: 300px; padding: 24px; border-radius: 8px; box-shadow: 0 2px 6px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1); } .card:hover { box-shadow: 0 8px 20px rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.25); } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **The new pieces:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `box-shadow` | A shadow drawn round the outside of the box. | | `0 2px 6px` | Three measurements, separated by spaces, always in this order: how far **right**, how far **down**, and how **blurred**. `0 2px 6px` means not sideways at all, 2 pixels down, blurred by 6. | | `rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.1)` | The shadow's colour. Now **move your mouse pointer on top of the card and leave it there**. Do not click. The haze underneath grows deeper and spreads further down, and the card appears to rise. 6. **Move the pointer off the card.** The shadow shrinks back to the faint version. Changed something since? It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. assignments.name: Transitions
assignments.description:
## Make a button change slowly, not instantly

**What you are making:** a button that eases from purple to blue and slides gently upwards when you point at it, instead of snapping. One line of CSS is the difference between a page that feels cheap and one that feels finished.

**Time:** about 25 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing.

---

### Before you start

You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how:

- **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen.
- **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code.


---

### Step 1 — Open your course folder

1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer.
2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**.
3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**.

*(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)*

### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder

The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are.

1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse.
2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**.
3. Click **Open Git Bash here**.

A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type.

*(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)*

> **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it.

### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer

At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-transitions-yourname`.

1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**).
2. Click on the black terminal window.
3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*:

```bash
git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS
```

4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working.
5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-transitions-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**:

```bash
cd webdev-css-transitions-YOUR_USERNAME
```

### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files

In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it:

```bash
code .
```

**VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.**

CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files:

- `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step)
- `style.css` — where you write your CSS

**To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file.

Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*:

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <meta charset="UTF-8" />
    <title>My page</title>
    <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />
  </head>
  <body>
  </body>
</html>
```

The `<link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `<body>` and `</body>` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`.

### Step 5 — Do the task

**Your goal:** make a button's hover change happen smoothly over a fifth of a second.

This has two halves. Do them in order.

**Half 1 — put the button on the page (in `index.html`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right.
2. Find the line that reads `</body>`. It is near the bottom.
3. Click at the end of the line **above** `</body>` and press **Enter** to make a new empty line.
4. Type this exactly:

```html
<button class="btn">Hover over me</button>
```

5. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*.

**Half 2 — make the change smooth (in `style.css`)**

1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**.
2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line.
3. Type this exactly:

```css
.btn {
  background-color: #6a11cb;
  color: white;
  border: none;
  padding: 12px 24px;
  border-radius: 8px;
  font-size: 16px;
  transition: all 0.2s ease;
}

.btn:hover {
  background-color: #2575fc;
  transform: translateY(-4px);
}
```

4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again.

**The new pieces:**

| Piece | What it means |
|---|---|
| `transition` | "Do not switch straight to the new look — travel to it." It goes on the **normal** rule, never on the `:hover` rule. This catches people out every time. |
| `all` | Which changes to travel through. `all` means every one of them. |
| `0.2s` | How long the journey takes. `s` means seconds, so this is two tenths of a second. |
| `ease` | The style of the journey: starts gently, speeds up, slows down at the end. |
| `transform: translateY(-4px);` | Move this thing. `translateY` means up and down, and **the minus sign means upwards**. Four pixels up. Nothing around it shifts to make room. |
| `padding: 12px 24px;` | Two measurements: 12 pixels of space above and below, 24 to the left and right. |

Read the two rules together. The `.btn` rule says what the button normally looks like *and how it travels*. The `.btn:hover` rule says where it travels **to**.

> You may change the two colour codes and the button's words. Keep the `transition` line on the `.btn` rule and the `:hover` on the second rule.

### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes

1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list.
2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*.
3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page.
4. You should see a purple button with rounded corners and white writing.
5. Now **move your mouse pointer on top of the button and leave it there**. Do not click. The purple does not switch to blue — it *fades* into blue, and the button glides about four pixels upwards at the same time. It takes about a fifth of a second.
6. **Move the pointer away.** It fades and glides back down, as smoothly as before.

If that felt too quick to be sure of, slow it right down:

7. Go back to VS Code, click the `style.css` tab, and change `0.2s` to `2s`.
8. Press **Ctrl + S**, click back to the browser, press **Ctrl + R** to reload, then point at the button again. Now the journey takes two full seconds and you can watch the colour crawl across. Put `0.2s` back afterwards — two seconds is far too slow for a real page.

The colour snaps instead of fading? The `transition` line is on the wrong rule. It belongs in `.btn`, not `.btn:hover`.

---

### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub

Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each:

```bash
git add .
git commit -m "Add a smooth hover transition"
git push
```

- `git add .` gathers everything you changed.
- `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached.
- `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.**

### Step 8 — Hand it in

```bash
git tag submit/1
git push origin submit/1
```

This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.*

### Step 9 — Check your result

Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see:

- ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson.
- ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**:

```bash
git tag submit/2
git push origin submit/2
```

Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again.

---

### If something goes wrong

| What you see | What it means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| The colour changes, but it snaps instantly | The `transition` line is inside the `:hover` rule | Move it up into the plain `.btn` rule. The transition lives on the normal state |
| Nothing happens at all when you point at it | The two rules use different names | `.btn` and `.btn:hover` must match, and the button must read `<button class="btn">` |
| The button moves down instead of up | The minus sign is missing | It is `translateY(-4px)`. Without the minus it travels downwards |
| Red cross on "uses transition" | The word is misspelled or the colon is missing | The line reads `transition: all 0.2s ease;` — word, colon, three values, semicolon |
| The button jumps around and pushes other things aside | `margin-top` was used instead of `transform` | `transform` moves the button without disturbing anything else. Use the line as written |
| `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see |
| `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again |
| `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder |

### Before you submit, check

- [ ] `style.css` contains `transition: all 0.2s ease;` inside the plain `.btn` rule
- [ ] `style.css` contains a `.btn:hover` rule
- [ ] The `:hover` rule changes the background colour and has `transform: translateY(-4px);`
- [ ] `index.html` has the `<button class="btn">` line
- [ ] Every line inside the curly brackets ends with `;`
- [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs)
- [ ] Pointing at the button makes it fade and glide rather than snap

## Stack your columns on a narrow screen **What you are making:** a page with two boxes side by side that drop into a single stack when the window gets narrow. One page, two shapes — this is how a website fits a laptop and a phone at the same time. **Time:** about 30 minutes. Go slowly — there is no prize for rushing. --- ### Before you start You need these open. If you have never opened them, the **Set up your computer** lesson shows you how: - **File Explorer** — the yellow folder icon on the bar at the bottom of your screen. - **VS Code** — the app with the blue icon where you type code. --- ### Step 1 — Open your course folder 1. Click the **yellow folder icon** on the bar at the bottom of your screen. This is **File Explorer** — it is how you look at folders on your computer. 2. On the left-hand side, click **Documents**. 3. Double-click the folder called **`lacefi-academy`**. *(On a Mac: open **Finder**, click **Documents**, open `lacefi-academy`.)* ### Step 2 — Open the terminal inside that folder The **terminal** is a window where you type instructions instead of clicking. Opening it *inside* your folder matters — it means the terminal already knows where you are. 1. **Right-click** on any empty white space inside the `lacefi-academy` folder. "Empty space" means somewhere with no file underneath your mouse. 2. A small menu appears. Click **Show more options**. 3. Click **Open Git Bash here**. A window opens with text and a blinking line. That blinking line is the computer waiting for you to type. *(On a Mac: press **Command + Space**, type `Terminal`, press **Enter**, then type `cd ~/Documents/lacefi-academy` and press **Enter**.)* > **Don't see "Open Git Bash here"?** Git Bash is not installed yet. Go back to the **Set up your computer** lesson and install it. ### Step 3 — Download this assignment to your computer At the **top of this assignment page** there is your own repository address. It looks something like `https://github.com/lacefi-academy/webdev-css-media-queries-yourname`. 1. Click that address once to select it, then copy it (**Ctrl + C**). 2. Click on the black terminal window. 3. Type `git clone`, then a space, then paste the address *(in Git Bash, right-click → Paste)*: ```bash git clone YOUR_REPOSITORY_ADDRESS ``` 4. Press **Enter**. Text scrolls past — that is the download working. 5. Move into the folder that just arrived. Type `cd webdev-css-media-queries-` then press the **Tab** key (the computer finishes the name for you), then press **Enter**: ```bash cd webdev-css-media-queries-YOUR_USERNAME ``` ### Step 4 — Open the project and create your files In the same terminal, type this and press **Enter**. The dot is part of it: ```bash code . ``` **VS Code opens.** This project starts almost empty — on the left you will see only a `README.md` (these instructions) and a hidden setup folder. **There are no code files yet — you create them yourself.** CSS styles a web page, so you make **two** files: - `index.html` — the page (you will add its contents in the next step) - `style.css` — where you write your CSS **To make each file:** move your mouse over the file list on the left, click the **New File** icon (a small page with a **+**), type the name exactly, and press **Enter**. Do this once for each file. Now **click `index.html`** in the file list, paste in this starting point exactly, and save with **Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*: ```html My page ``` The `` line is already here for you — it connects your stylesheet to the page. The space between `` and `` is where the next step has you add the page's content; your styling goes in `style.css`. ### Step 5 — Do the task **Your goal:** put two boxes side by side, then tell the browser to stack them whenever there is not enough room. This has two halves. Do them in order. **Half 1 — make the two boxes (in `index.html`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `index.html`**. It opens in the big area on the right. 2. Near the top of the file, find the line that says ``. Click at the end of that line and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this one line. It is long — let it run off the edge of the screen and do not press **Enter** in the middle of it: ```html ``` That line tells a phone to admit how wide it really is. Without it, a phone pretends to be a wide desktop and everything else in this task is ignored on the very devices it was written for. 4. Now find the line that says `` and the line that says ``. Click at the end of a line between them and press **Enter**. 5. Type these four lines, one under the other: ```html
Column one
Column two
``` 6. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. The outer box is labelled `layout`. The two boxes inside it are both labelled `box` — a class may be used as many times as you like on one page. **Half 2 — the wide rule, then the narrow rule (in `style.css`)** 1. In the file list on the left of VS Code, **click once on `style.css`**. 2. Click at the very bottom of whatever is already in the file and press **Enter** for a new line. 3. Type this exactly. Mind the brackets near the end — there are three closing brackets, and every one is needed: ```css .layout { display: flex; gap: 20px; } .box { width: 50%; padding: 20px; background-color: lightblue; } @media (max-width: 700px) { .layout { flex-direction: column; } .box { width: 100%; } } ``` 4. **Save the file: press Ctrl + S** *(Mac: Command + S)*. If the tab at the top of VS Code shows a white dot instead of an ✕, it is **not saved** — press Ctrl + S again. **What each piece means:** | Piece | What it means | |---|---| | `display: flex;` | Lays the boxes inside `.layout` out in a row, side by side. | | `gap: 20px;` | A 20-dot space between them. | | `@media` | "Only under certain conditions." Every rule inside it is switched off until the condition is true. | | `(max-width: 700px)` | The condition: the window is **at most** 700 dots wide. Read it as "while the window is 700 dots or narrower". | | `flex-direction: column;` | Turns that row into a stack, one box above the other. | | `width: 100%;` | Once stacked, each box takes the full width rather than half of it. | **About the brackets.** `@media` has a pair of curly brackets of its own, and each rule inside has its own pair as well. So the end of the file has three `}` in a row, each on its own line, stepping back towards the left. Leave one out and the browser discards the whole block without a word of complaint. > You may change the words inside the boxes, the colour, and the number `700`. `@media`, `max-width` and `flex-direction: column;` must stay exactly as written. ### Step 6 — See it working with your own eyes 1. In VS Code, **right-click `index.html`** in the file list. 2. Click **Reveal in File Explorer** *(Mac: **Reveal in Finder**)*. 3. In the window that opens, **double-click `index.html`**. Your web browser opens and shows your page. 4. You should see two light blue boxes **side by side**, with a gap between them. A media query only shows what it does when the window **changes size**. So now change the size of the window by hand. 5. Look at the **top-right corner** of the browser window. There are three small buttons: **—**, a square, and **✕**. Click the **middle** one. The window shrinks away from the edges of the screen, so there is now room to pull it about. *(Mac: if the window fills the screen, press **Control + Command + F** first.)* 6. Move the mouse pointer slowly onto the **right-hand edge** of the browser window — the very border, where the window stops. The pointer changes shape into a double-headed arrow. That shape means "this edge can be dragged". 7. **Press and hold** the left mouse button. Do not let go yet. 8. Still holding, move the mouse steadily to the **left**. The window gets narrower as you go. 9. Keep watching the two blue boxes while you drag. At the moment the window becomes narrower than 700 dots the boxes **jump**. You cannot see that number anywhere, so drag slowly and watch for the change: instead of sitting side by side they are now one above the other, each one running the full width. 10. Let go of the mouse button. Then drag that same edge back out to the right. The boxes hop back into a row. That jump is your media query switching on and off. Nothing reloaded and nothing was retyped — the same page carries two shapes at once. Changed something since? Save with **Ctrl + S**, then click back to the browser and press **Ctrl + R** to reload. They never stack, however narrow you drag? Count the closing brackets at the bottom of `style.css` — there must be three. --- ### Step 7 — Save your work to GitHub Go back to the black terminal window. Type these **one at a time**, pressing **Enter** after each: ```bash git add . git commit -m "Stack columns on narrow screens" git push ``` - `git add .` gathers everything you changed. - `git commit -m "..."` saves a snapshot with a note attached. - `git push` uploads it to GitHub. **This saves your work. It does not grade it.** ### Step 8 — Hand it in ```bash git tag submit/1 git push origin submit/1 ``` This tells the checker: *please mark my work now.* ### Step 9 — Check your result Come back to this assignment page and refresh it. After a minute you will see: - ✅ **green check** — you passed. Move on to the next lesson. - ❌ **red cross** — something is missing. Fix it, repeat **Step 7**, then hand in again using the **next number**: ```bash git tag submit/2 git push origin submit/2 ``` Keep going — `submit/3`, `submit/4` — until it is green. There is no penalty for trying again. --- ### If something goes wrong | What you see | What it means | What to do | |---|---|---| | The boxes never stack, however narrow the window | A closing bracket is missing, so the browser discarded the media query | `style.css` must end with three `}` lines, one under the other | | The boxes are stacked even when the window is wide | You typed `min-width` where the task says `max-width` | `max-width` means "at most this wide" — change it back | | The boxes are one above the other from the very start | `.layout` has no `display: flex;` | Add `display: flex;` inside the `.layout` rule, above the media query | | The window will not get any narrower | The window is maximised — pinned to the edges of the screen | Click the **middle button of the three** at the top-right corner first, then drag the edge | | Red cross on "uses a media query" | The `@` is missing, or `style.css` was not saved | The line must begin `@media`. Press **Ctrl + S**, then repeat Step 7 | | `bash: cd: No such file or directory` | You are not in the folder you think you are | Type `ls` and press **Enter** to see what is around you, then `cd` into the name you see | | `git push` asks for a username or password | The GitHub CLI is not logged in | Type `gh auth login` and answer the questions, then try again | | `code` is not recognised | VS Code is not linked to the terminal | Open VS Code from the Start menu instead, then **File → Open Folder** and pick your assignment folder | ### Before you submit, check - [ ] `style.css` contains a line beginning `@media` - [ ] The condition on that line reads `(max-width: 700px)` - [ ] `.layout` has `display: flex;` - [ ] Inside the media query, `.layout` has `flex-direction: column;` - [ ] `style.css` ends with three `}` lines, one under the other - [ ] Both files are saved (no white dots on the VS Code tabs) - [ ] You have dragged the window narrow and watched the boxes stack
